analysis.one_liner: Requires hospitals and insurers to publish their real negotiated prices for care and drugs.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan hospital and insurer price transparency bill was introduced in March 2023 and never received a committee vote before the two-year Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would write hospital price disclosure rules into law: hospitals would have to publish, in a searchable consumer-friendly format, the rates they negotiate with each insurer, their discounted cash prices, and billing codes for at least 300 common schedulable services. Health insurance plans would have to publish in-network and out-of-network rates for covered services and the net prices they actually pay for prescription drugs, and offer a free online tool letting patients look up what a service would cost them before they get it. The bill never advanced past its committee assignment.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients with hospital or commercial insurance coverage, and uninsured people paying cash, who could see real negotiated and cash prices before receiving care, comparison-shop across providers, and see the net price insurers pay for prescription drugs after rebates.

how_it_helps.text: Hospitals must publish, in plain language and machine-readable form, the payer-specific negotiated charge, minimum and maximum negotiated charges, discounted cash price, gross charge, and billing codes for at least 300 schedulable 'shoppable' services [S3].

Hospitals can satisfy the disclosure duty by maintaining a free, public internet price-estimator tool that gives consumers a real-time estimate of what they will owe, searchable by service, billing code, and payer, with no personal information required [S3].

Health plans must disclose in-network rates, out-of-network allowed amounts, and the negotiated rates and historical net prices for prescription drugs, and provide a free self-service online tool (plus paper lookups on request) so patients can estimate their cost-sharing in advance [S3].

The bill extends the insurance transparency requirements beyond Obamacare marketplace plans to all group health plans, including self-insured employer plans, so most people with job-based coverage get the same price information [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals, health insurers, and pharmacy benefit managers, who would have to reveal negotiated rates, rebate-inclusive drug prices, and out-of-network payments, losing pricing opacity that lets different patients pay widely different amounts for the same care. Compliance costs would fall on the same entities.

drawbacks.text: The bill's only new penalty is a civil monetary fine capped at $300 per day of ongoing violation, far below typical hospital revenues, so enforcement pressure is weak; this mirrors the fine critics say made the existing hospital price rule easy to ignore [S3].

Estimates are not guarantees: the bill requires plans to warn consumers that actual charges may differ and that an estimate of cost-sharing is not a promise of coverage, so a patient can still be surprised by the final bill [S3].

Publishing all negotiated rates could make it harder for insurers and providers to strike confidential discounts, and industry groups have argued the transparency mandates impose significant compliance costs that could be passed into premiums [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is real but indirect: price disclosure does not lower prices by itself, it only enables shopping and public pressure, and the $300-a-day penalty cap limits how strictly hospitals can be forced to comply. Still, the cost of the bill is mostly compliance expense at large hospital systems and insurers, while the information it unlocks is exactly what patients need to avoid surprise bills and compare prices.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate bill was read twice and referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never took it up, so it died there when the two-year Congress ended in early January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Mike Braun introduced the Health Care PRICE Transparency Act in the Senate on March 30, 2023, joined by Sen. Chuck Grassley as its sole cosponsor [S1][S3][S4].
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions; no further action was ever recorded on it [S5].
The bill would have amended the Public Health Service Act and the Affordable Care Act to put hospital and insurer price-disclosure requirements into statute [S3].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, with the bill still sitting in committee, so it received no committee vote, no floor vote, and no companion action record in the House [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals, health insurers, and pharmacy benefit managers are better off because the bill died: they keep the ability to negotiate confidential rates without having to publish negotiated charges, drug net prices, or out-of-network payments. Patients remain reliant on federal agency rules rather than statute for any price disclosure.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hospitals and insurers kept price opacity

sides.party_line_note: The bill's two Senate sponsors were both Republicans and it never drew a recorded vote or public opposition, so no partisan split can be measured; it simply never left committee.

industries.note: Hospitals would have had to publish every insurer's negotiated rate, their cash discount price, and billing codes for at least 300 common services, ending the chargemaster opacity that lets the same procedure cost patients wildly different amounts. Hospital groups have resisted statutory disclosure mandates and the bill's weak $300-per-day penalty suggests they had leverage over the design.

Insurers would have had to publish in-network and out-of-network rates for all covered services and offer a free real-time cost-estimator tool, extending these duties from marketplace plans to employer and self-insured plans. Price opacity is central to how plans negotiate and market coverage, so mandatory disclosure narrows their flexibility.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and drug pricing intermediaries
industries.note: Plans would have had to disclose the historical net price of prescription drugs including allocated rebates, discounts, and fees, exposing how much of a drug's list price never reaches consumers. PBMs profit on the spread between list and net prices, which this disclosure would make visible.
